Polynomial homotopy theories force the polynomial path ring to be contractible; ordinary algebraic \(K\)-theory can retain its Nil contribution. The kernel of evaluation at one on \(tA[t]\) is \(t(t-1)A[t]\).
reconstruction: The modern \(NK\) notation distinguishes these groups from differently indexed categories of nilpotent endomorphisms. The equality with a nonunital absolute functor is not used as an assertion of excision for arbitrary ideals.
fate: \citet[third theorem, p.231]{vaserstein1973foundations} states the polynomial and Laurent decompositions with these Nil terms. The distinction from polynomial-path \(K\)-theory is discussed in \citet[Introduction, p.96]{vaserstein1976foundations}; the underlying Karoubi--Villamayor theory had circulated before the lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026: established distinction; Nil groups are exactly the obstruction in this polynomial splitting, not an omission to be discarded for every ring.

title: Relative groups and the correction from kernels to fibre products
notes: The source first writes \(K_{n+1}(A)=K_n(A'')\) after calling \(A''\) the kernel of a free presentation. It later proposes a pullback ring \(F\) giving an exact sequence \(\cdots\to K_n(A)\to K_n(B)\to K_n(F)\to K_{n-1}(A)\to\cdots\), with an ambiguous \(\mu B\)-label on an inclusion into \(\ell B\).
statement: For a homomorphism \(f:A\to B\), define relative \(K\)-theory by the homotopy fibre of \(K(A)\to K(B)\); its groups fit \(\cdots\to K_n(A,B)\to K_n(A)\to K_n(B)\to K_{n-1}(A,B)\to\cdots\). In Vaserstein's ring model let \(F(B)\to B\) be the free nonunital presentation and put \(D_f=A\times_B F(B)\). His relative group is represented by \(K_n(D_f)\). For dimension shifting he uses \(D(A)=F(A)\times_A F(A)\), with \(K_n(D(A))\cong K_{n+1}(A)\).
reconstruction: The fibre sequence fixes the indexing: a ring sitting after \(K_n(B)\) in the notes represents a shifted relative object. The published doubled fibre product is not simply the presentation kernel. The drawn inclusion cannot have the earlier quotient \(\mu B\) as its evident source; its uncertain letter is left unresolved, and the verified published model is supplied separately.
fate: \citet[second theorem, p.231]{vaserstein1973foundations} gives the relative pullback model. \citet[\S20, Theorem 29.1 and its proof, pp.142--143]{vaserstein1976foundations} identifies the doubled fibre product and proves dimension shifting. General excision is not assumed.
present_status: As of November 2026: established relative and dimension-shift constructions. The literal kernel recursion and the unqualified pullback diagram are not sufficient definitions.

title: The plus construction does not automatically make every group an H-space
notes: For any group \(G\) with perfect commutator subgroup \(E\), the notes attach cells to \(BG\), kill \(E\), preserve homology, and say that this turns the result into a group or H-space.
statement: The plus construction \(BG\to BG_E^+\) kills the specified perfect normal subgroup and preserves homology with the appropriate local coefficients. This operation alone does not provide an H-space multiplication for every such \(G\). For the stable general linear group, compatible block sums supply the additional multiplication, and Quillen's positive groups are \(\pi_n(BGL(A)^+)\).
reconstruction: The general existence of plus is separated from the stable-linear source of its multiplication. Homotopy groups of a general plus space are not automatically ring \(K\)-groups without a ring and the relevant model.
fate: Quillen's already circulated account \citep[\S3, p.50]{quillen1971cohomology} treats the stable general linear group and its coherent categorical structure. The general plus theorem is given with its correct hypotheses in \citet[IV, Theorem 1.5]{weibel2013kbook}.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard after this distinction; the universal H-space claim is an overstatement in the notebook.

title: The assertion that everything extends to the unitary case
notes: One emphatic sentence says that everything carries over to the unitary case.
statement: The preceding discussion contains several inequivalent assertions: plus constructions, comparison of models, suspension, relative groups, and Laurent decompositions. A unitary or hermitian version must specify a ring with involution, symmetry and form parameter, degree conventions, and often additional hypotheses. None is supplied by this sentence.
reconstruction: It is therefore not interpreted as a single theorem asserting all earlier formulas unchanged for every hermitian theory. It continues the programme of record 246, rather than settling every possible hermitian analogue.
fate: The verified \citet{vaserstein1973foundations,vaserstein1976foundations} concern ordinary algebraic \(K\)-theory. Their linear comparison theorem does not verify this unrestricted unitary extension. The earlier form-ring work \citep{vaserstein1970stabilization} supports the setting but not the claimed all-degree package.
present_status: As of November 2026: the exact package intended remains underdetermined; no claim that hermitian \(K\)-theory itself was left undeveloped is made.

title: The higher Laurent fundamental theorem and its missing summands
notes: A theorem attributed to an uncertain surname resembling Wagoner is written \(K_2(A[t,t^{-1}])=K_2(A)\oplus K_1(A)\oplus ?\). It is asserted for all \(n\), with the other degrees following from this case.
statement: For a unital associative ring and central Laurent variable, the nonconnective fundamental theorem is \[K_n(A[t,t^{-1}])\cong K_n(A)\oplus K_{n-1}(A)\oplus NK_n(A)\oplus NK_n(A),\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.\] For regular noetherian \(A\), the two Nil groups vanish. The constant inclusion is split by evaluation at \(t=1\); it does not make the remaining relative group zero.
reconstruction: The circled final mark remains a question mark diplomatically; the two Nil terms are supplied from the precise theorem. The arrow from \(A\) means inclusion as constant polynomials, not the coefficient-extraction map from Laurent polynomials, which is not a ring homomorphism.
fate: The full formula occurs in \citet[third theorem, p.231]{vaserstein1973foundations}. Its prior low-degree antecedents are \citet{basshellerswan1964whitehead,gersten1971laurent}. Wagoner is a plausible reading of the name, supported by the contemporary suspension literature, but the scan does not identify a precise cited paper; no priority claim rests on that reading.
present_status: As of November 2026: established, with two Nil terms for general rings. The claim that a written relative \(K_2\) is simply trivial requires correction.

title: Whitehead’s four factors and the Laurent K1-to-K2 class
notes: The diagonal block \(\operatorname{diag}(a,a^{-1})\) is written as four elementary matrices, with two entries left as dots. The notes then place the diagonal blocks for \(gt\), \(t\), and \(g\) side by side, and say that their elementary decompositions give a relation, hence an element of \(K_2\).
statement: For an invertible matrix \(a\), put \(U(b)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) and \(L(c)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\c&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Then \(\operatorname{diag}(a,a^{-1})=U(a-1)L(1)U(a^{-1}-1)L(-a)\). If \(h(a)\) is the corresponding Steinberg lift and \(t\) is central, the product \(h(gt)h(t)^{-1}h(g)^{-1}\) maps to the identity and so defines a \(K_2(A[t,t^{-1}])\)-class. With compatible conventions this is the Laurent splitting from \(K_1(A)\).
reconstruction: The two entries are uniquely recovered by multiplication. The inverses and multiplication order between the three lifts are supplied; without them the three displayed matrices do not themselves constitute a relation. Well-definedness on \(K_1\) is part of the established splitting theorem, not proved by the shorthand alone.
fate: The elementary identity is Whitehead's classical stabilization device. The low-degree Laurent map is part of the theory discussed in \citet{milnor1972introduction,gersten1971laurent}; the full splitting is explicitly recorded by \citet[third theorem]{vaserstein1973foundations}. Milnor's book was published in January 1972 according to the publisher catalogue.
present_status: As of November 2026: established. The restored factors are an elementary verification of the written construction, not a new research contribution.

title: Compression of Laurent relations and the inverse boundary
notes: For the converse, Laurent multiplication is made into an infinite matrix, cut to one side, and considered modulo finite matrices. The quotient is written \(\ell A/\mu A\), although \(\mu A\) was previously the quotient ring.
statement: Laurent polynomial matrices act as two-sided finite-band matrices. Compression to nonnegative indices is a ring homomorphism modulo the ideal of finitely supported matrices, because the multiplication defect has finite support. A \(K_2\)-relation can be lifted through the resulting extension; its boundary is a \(K_1(A)\)-class after Morita identification of the finite-matrix ideal. The quotient intended with the earlier notation is \(\ell A/MA=\mu A\).
reconstruction: The method is the preceding record's truncation construction, now used in the reverse Laurent map. The word Laurent series cannot automatically mean arbitrary formal series: their matrices need not belong to the row-and-column-finite algebra being used. The safe algebraic domain here is Laurent polynomials or an explicitly enlarged topological matrix algebra, not supplied by the notes.
fate: The precise suspension and exact-sequence context is \citet[first--third theorems]{vaserstein1973foundations} and \citet[\S\S18--20]{vaserstein1976foundations}. The notebook supplies an implementation sketch, so the publication match is partial.
present_status: As of November 2026: established as the algebraic boundary after the matrix class and ideal are fixed; the notation drift is not a new quotient construction.

title: Vaserstein’s explicit expectation of agreement with Quillen
notes: After the pullback construction, the notebook says \ru{По мнению Л. В. теория Квиллена совпадает с этими}: in Vaserstein's opinion Quillen's theory agrees with these. The next line explicitly excludes Karoubi's polynomial theory.
statement: For an associative ring \(A\) with identity, the stable Volodin--Vaserstein simplicial groups and the free-resolution groups of Swan and Gersten should be naturally isomorphic to \(K_n^Q(A)=\pi_nBGL(A)^+\) for every \(n\ge1\). The comparison does not assert agreement with Karoubi--Villamayor groups for arbitrary singular rings.
reconstruction: The positive index range and unital hypothesis identify the exact theorem later published. The notation does not make an unrestricted assertion about all nonunital or polynomial-homotopy constructions.
fate: The expectation is stated as a theorem in the comparison block assigned conditionally to record 257. \citet[first theorem, p.231]{vaserstein1973foundations} announces the agreement, and \citet[\S27, Theorem 27.2; \S29, Theorem 29.1]{vaserstein1976foundations} gives the detailed comparisons. The latter explicitly dates first announcement to Gelfand's seminar in spring 1972; the short article was received on 14 November 1972.
present_status: As of November 2026: resolved in the stated scope. GP-1971-21 links this conjectural wording, the suspension question in 1971-256.3, and the comparison theorem in 1971-257.2.

title: Projections onto a Laurent-series lattice and a finite-rank commutator
notes: The source sets \(K=k((t))\), \(A=k[[t]]\), and chooses maps \(p_1+p_2=1\), \(p_1A=0\), \(p_2K\subset A\). For \(f,g\in K\) it writes the trace of a commutator with uncertain projection subscripts and calls the operator finite rank.
statement: Let \(P:K\to A\) be a \(k\)-linear projection with \(P|_A=1\), and define \(T_f=P\circ M_f|_A\), where \(M_f\) is multiplication by \(f\). The commutator \([T_f,T_g]\) is finite rank on \(A\): its two multiplication defects factor through the finite-dimensional quotients \((A+fA)/A\) and \((A+gA)/A\). Hence its ordinary finite-rank trace is defined. If one instead works on all of \(K\), Tate's finite-potent trace is the appropriate general construction; a full-space compressed commutator need not itself have finite rank.
reconstruction: The stated conditions force \(p_2\) to be a projection onto \(A\); thus \(P=p_2\) is a natural modern convention. Compression to \(A\), the multiplication notation, and the distinction between finite-rank and finite-potent operators are supplied rather than read into the uncertain final subscripts.
fate: \citet[\S1 and \S2, Theorem 1, pp.149--152]{tate1968residues} defines the trace and the abstract residue. The present compressed formula is a specialization of that theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026: established for the formal Laurent field over any ground field. No analytic Hilbert-space trace or characteristic-zero restriction is needed.

title: Tate’s coordinate-free formula for the residue
notes: The question asks for the residue of \(f\,dg\); the parenthetical phrase most plausibly says ``without a parameter''. The trace construction is the proposed answer.
statement: With the preceding convention, \[\operatorname{res}_{t=0}(f\,dg)=\operatorname{Tr}_A([T_f,T_g]).\] The value is independent of the projection and of the chosen uniformizer of the discrete valuation ring \(A\). With the standard projection onto nonnegative powers it equals the coefficient of \(t^{-1}\) in \(f(t)g'(t)\). The normalization is \(\operatorname{res}(t^{-1}dt)=1\); on \(A\), the backward-shift/forward-shift commutator is the projection onto constants.
reconstruction: The projection convention and commutator order fix the sign. Parameter independence is inferred as the intended question from Tate's exact matching construction, while the notebook's parenthesis remains diplomatically qualified. No global residue theorem is attributed to this short remark.
fate: The coordinate-free theorem is \citet[Theorem 1 and property (R1), pp.151--152; Theorem 2, p.155]{tate1968residues}. Tate states that it grew from a Bowdoin lecture in summer 1967; publication was in 1968, well before Kazhdan's report.
present_status: As of November 2026: classical and fully resolved. The notebook is an economical exposition of the trace interpretation, not evidence for an orphan residue problem.

title: The simplex category, simplicial objects, and realization
notes: The auxiliary category has objects \([n]=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\); the displayed monotonicity condition starts at \(\varphi(1)\). A boxed insertion says contravariant. The realization glues the pieces \(A_n\times\Delta^n\). Gelfand's name is written by this explanation.
statement: Let \(\Delta\) have finite nonempty ordered sets \([n]\) as objects and all order-preserving maps as morphisms, so \(\varphi(0)\le\cdots\le\varphi(k)\). A simplicial object in \(\mathcal C\) is a functor \(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal C\). For a simplicial set \(A\), its geometric realization is \(\coprod_{n\ge0}A_n\times\Delta^n\) modulo the face and degeneracy identifications. It is a CW complex, generally not a simplicial complex without subdivision.
reconstruction: The omitted endpoint in the monotonicity condition and the distinction between simplicial sets and complexes are restored. The named Gabriel--Zisman reference is contextual, not an additional mathematical assertion.
fate: These constructions are given in \citet[\S1, pp.105--106]{segal1968classifying}, received in April 1967 and published in 1968; they predate this explanatory intervention.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard simplicial language, with the contravariance explicitly supported by the notebook's own insertion.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand, during Morava’s exposition

title: The nerve of a category and the group classifying space
notes: The notes identify zero-simplices with objects, one-simplices with morphisms, and higher simplices with composable chains. A one-object groupoid gives \(BC_n=G^n\), and realization is compared with Milnor's \(BG\).
statement: For a small category \(\mathcal C\), define \(N_n\mathcal C\) as strings of \(n\) composable arrows. Faces compose adjacent arrows or omit an endpoint; degeneracies insert identities. Set \(B\mathcal C=|N_\bullet\mathcal C|\). If \(\mathcal C\) has one object and automorphism group a discrete group \(G\), then \(N_n\mathcal C=G^n\) and \(B\mathcal C\) is a \(K(G,1)\). For a topological group one uses a topological nerve and suitable well-behaved realization; higher homotopy need not vanish.
reconstruction: The source uses \(BC\) for both the simplicial object and its realization. Distinct notation prevents confusing these, and the discrete/topological distinction is retained.
fate: \citet[\S\S2--3, pp.106--107]{segal1968classifying} gives exactly the categorical nerve, the one-object group example, and the comparison with Milnor's classifying space, including topological qualifications.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard. The one-object description does not identify topological \(BG\) with an Eilenberg--MacLane space unless the group is discrete.

title: Products of nerves and natural isomorphisms as homotopies
notes: The lemma states \(B(\alpha\times\beta)=B\alpha\times B\beta\). Direct sum induces multiplication, but \(M\oplus N\) and \(N\oplus M\) are isomorphic rather than literally equal. A shuffle picture explains homotopy commutativity.
statement: The nerve preserves categorical products, and geometric realization preserves products in compactly generated spaces. A natural transformation of functors induces a homotopy between the corresponding maps of classifying spaces. Consequently the direct-sum functor on the groupoid of finitely generated projective modules makes its classifying space a homotopy-commutative and homotopy-associative H-space, with unit supplied by the zero module; the standard associativity and symmetry isomorphisms carry the coherent data.
reconstruction: The ambient category of spaces and the natural-transformation mechanism are supplied. A chosen product triangulation or shuffle model realizes this mechanism; no strict equality of the two functors is asserted.
fate: \citet[\S1 and Proposition 2.1, p.106]{segal1968classifying} proves product preservation and the homotopy induced by a natural transformation. The coherently additive categorical construction is developed in \citet[\S2]{segal1974categories}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established; the notebook correctly distinguishes equality of objects from canonical isomorphism.

title: Strict commutative multiplication and generalized Eilenberg–MacLane spaces
notes: A remark says that strictly commutative and associative multiplication, rather than multiplication only up to homotopy, makes \(X\) a product of \(K(\pi_n,n)\). A nearby box says ``Boardman--Vogt 1968 unpublished''. No unit, inverses, or topological regularity are specified in the displayed implication.
statement: A safe precise version is that a topological abelian group, after passage to its singular simplicial abelian group, has the weak homotopy type of a product of Eilenberg--MacLane spaces, noncanonically. For CW-type models this gives the corresponding homotopy equivalence. Such a conclusion for a raw binary associative commutative operation requires at least the relevant unit, group-completion, and topological hypotheses; a bare operation does not specify them.
reconstruction: The statement is restricted to the standard abelian-group model and is a homotopy-type assertion, not a homeomorphism or a canonical splitting. The Boardman--Vogt note cannot be taken as evidence that no announcement had been published by 1972.
fate: \citet[Introduction, p.293]{segal1974categories} explains that the topological-abelian-group construction yields ordinary-cohomology summands. Separately, \citet[p.1117]{boardmanvogt1968homotopy} already published their recognition announcement in November 1968, while promising full details elsewhere.
present_status: As of November 2026: the precise classical statement is established. The notebook's omitted structural assumptions and its unpublished label need qualification.

title: Coherent commutativity and repeated delooping
notes: The theorem assumes multiplication commutative and associative ``in a canonical way'', constructs \(BX\) with the same structure, and iterates. It states \(B^k\mathcal C\simeq\Omega B^{k+1}\mathcal C\) for \(k\ge2\).
statement: A special \(\Gamma\)-space \(A\) has \(A(0)\) contractible and Segal equivalences \(A(n)\simeq A(1)^n\), compatible with all structure maps. Its iterated classifying spaces form a connective spectrum. The map \(A(1)\to\Omega BA(1)\) is an equivalence when \(\pi_0A(1)\) is a group under multiplication; otherwise it is the group-completion map. Later deloopings are connected and have the required inverse structure. Equivalently, a grouplike coherently commutative H-space of CW type is an infinite loop space.
reconstruction: The phrase ``canonical way'' is interpreted as full coherent structure, not merely one associating homotopy and one commuting homotopy. The group-completion condition accounts for why the initial category space is excluded from the notebook's eventual loop equivalences.
fate: \citet[Theorem A]{boardmanvogt1968homotopy} states the grouplike recognition and repeated-classifying-space theorem. Quillen reports Segal's categorical cohomology construction in \citet[\S3, p.50]{quillen1971cohomology}; the detailed \(\Gamma\)-space version is \citet[Definitions 1.1--1.3 and Proposition 1.4]{segal1974categories}.
present_status: As of November 2026: established. The principal claim predates the lecture, despite the later appearance of Segal's full paper.

title: The represented cohomology theory and its grading
notes: The notes write \(K_{\mathcal C}^{-k}(Y)=\lim_i[Y,\Omega^iB^{k+i}\mathcal C]\), equivalently a suspended-source formula, and say the limit is unnecessary after the displayed loop equivalences.
statement: If \(E\) is the associated spectrum with spaces \(E_r\) and coherent structure maps, its reduced cohomology on a finite based CW complex is \(\widetilde E^j(Y)=\varinjlim_r[\Sigma^rY,E_{r+j}]_*\), with nonnegative indices after increasing \(r\). For an \(\Omega\)-spectrum the transition maps are bijections and one may use a single sufficiently high level. For general CW complexes the definition is the stable mapping group \([\Sigma^\infty Y,\Sigma^jE]\). In particular \(E^{-n}(\mathrm{pt})=\pi_nE\) in the unreduced theory.
reconstruction: The displayed minus sign, the indexing of \(B\mathcal C\) as the nerve versus the first spectrum level, and the point/basepoint convention are not consistent enough to retain literally. The standard spectrum grading is supplied and kept separate from the notebook's \(K^{-k}\) notation.
fate: The construction is announced in \citet[\S3]{quillen1971cohomology} and made precise in \citet[\S1 and Propositions 3.3--3.4]{segal1974categories}. The equivalence after delooping is Proposition 1.4 of the latter paper.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard represented generalized cohomology. Stabilization is removed only after an appropriate loop-spectrum replacement, not for every initial category nerve.

title: Projective modules, automorphism groupoids, and algebraic K-theory
notes: The category is explicitly restricted to finitely generated projective \(R\)-modules and isomorphisms. Its classifying space is written as a disjoint union of \(K(GL(M),1)\); the resulting K-functor agrees with Quillen's.
statement: Choose a small skeleton of the groupoid \(\mathcal P(R)^{\simeq}\) of finitely generated projective right \(R\)-modules and isomorphisms. Then \(B\mathcal P(R)^{\simeq}\simeq\coprod_{[P]}B\operatorname{Aut}_R(P)\). Direct-sum group completion has zeroth space \(K_0(R)\times BGL(R)^+\), and its positive homotopy groups are Quillen's \(K_n(R)\). The sum ranges over isomorphism classes, and \(GL(M)\) here means the automorphism group of a projective module, not necessarily a free-module matrix group.
reconstruction: A skeleton, group completion, and the notation for module automorphisms are specified. Taking all module morphisms instead would introduce a zero object and a contractible nerve; the source's restriction to isomorphisms is therefore essential and is preserved.
fate: Quillen already states the projective-module categorical interpretation in \citet[\S3, p.50]{quillen1971cohomology}. \citet[\S2 and \S4, p.305]{segal1974categories} gives the group-completion model explicitly.
present_status: As of November 2026: established for unital associative rings. The uncompleted disjoint union itself is not yet the full K-theory space.

title: Finite sets and the Barratt–Priddy–Quillen theorem
notes: For the category of finite sets, the notes write \(B\mathcal C=\coprod_nB\Sigma_n\), and say the associated groups are stable cohomotopy. The entire union is called an H-space.
statement: Use the groupoid of finite sets and bijections, with disjoint union. Its nerve is \(\coprod_{n\ge0}B\Sigma_n\). Its group-completion spectrum is equivalent to the sphere spectrum \(\mathbb S\); equivalently its zeroth infinite loop space is \(QS^0\simeq\mathbb Z\times B\Sigma_\infty^+\). Thus the associated cohomology is stable cohomotopy. The category of finite sets and all functions has a terminal object and would not give this result by its plain nerve.
reconstruction: The morphisms are recovered from the displayed symmetric-group decomposition. Group completion and the missing component group \(\mathbb Z\) are made explicit.
fate: \citet[Proposition 3.5 and \S4]{segal1974categories} proves the stated sphere-spectrum result and credits Barratt--Priddy--Quillen. Its references identify prior Barratt and Priddy announcements in 1971; the notebook itself calls the result known. The full Segal proof was received in August 1972 and published in 1974.
present_status: As of November 2026: classical Barratt--Priddy--Quillen theorem, with the correct groupoid and completion specified.

title: Linearization from finite sets to free modules
notes: A finite set of size \(k\) is sent to \(R^k\), giving a map from stable cohomotopy to \(K(R)\). At a point this gives homomorphisms from stable homotopy groups of spheres to K-groups of every ring.
statement: The functor \(S\mapsto R[S]\), with bijections acting by permutation matrices, is compatible with disjoint union and direct sum. After group completion it induces a natural spectrum map \(\mathbb S\to K(R)\), sending \(1\in\pi_0\mathbb S\cong\mathbb Z\) to \([R]\in K_0(R)\). Consequently it induces \(\pi_n^S\to K_n(R)\) in all nonnegative degrees and the corresponding natural transformation on represented cohomology.
reconstruction: The map is interpreted as the spectrum map selected by the rank-one free module. For a general noncommutative ring no commutative ring-spectrum structure on \(K(R)\) is assumed.
fate: This follows within Segal's categorical functorial construction \citep[\S\S2--3, Proposition 3.5]{segal1974categories}; the prior announcement of the machine is \citet[\S3]{quillen1971cohomology}. The actual finite-set functor is explicitly present in the notebook.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard linearization. Its image need not be the whole K-group.

title: The unresolved image-of-J comparison over a prime field
notes: For \(R=\mathbb F_p\) and \(Y\) a point, a damaged relation sign connects \(K(R)^kY\) with ``image of the j-homomorphism''. Degrees, localization, and the map being compared are not supplied.
statement: The preceding linearization gives a definite map \(\pi_n^S\to K_n(\mathbb F_p)\), but the sentence does not specify whether its image, a quotient, a prime-local summand, or the entire target is meant. Equality of every target K-group with the image of this map is false: in degree one the permutation matrices have determinant only \(\pm1\), whereas \(K_1(\mathbb F_5)=\mathbb F_5^\times\) has order four.
reconstruction: The degree-one check separates a literal surjectivity reading from more refined relations with stable \(J\), which require prime and degree conventions. No one of those deeper formulations is selected as the intended missing theorem.
fate: The source's link to Quillen's finite-field computation is clear \citep[\S3, Theorems 1--2]{quillen1971cohomology}; Segal's verified paper establishes the sphere-spectrum and linearization framework but does not supply this particular image-of-\(J\) claim. Searches combining Morava, Segal, finite-field K-theory and image \(J\) gave related theorems without recovering the lost qualifiers.
present_status: As of November 2026: the exact comparison remains unidentified from the notebook. This is not an assertion that the classical image-of-\(J\) problem is open.

title: Triangular simplices on the stable general linear group
notes: An abstract simplicial scheme is a collection of finite subsets closed under passage to subsets. On stable matrices the notes declare a finite set \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) to be a simplex if simultaneous left and right multiplication by invertible matrices makes them upper unitriangular. Conjugates, permutation matrices, and a marginal reference to Volodin accompany \(K_i(A)=\pi_{i-1}GL(A)\).
statement: For an associative unital ring \(A\), one equips the set \(GL(A)=\varinjlim_nGL_n(A)\) with the triangular simplicial structure, rather than its discrete topology. A finite subset contained in a translate of an admissible conjugate of a unitriangular subgroup determines a simplex. In the usual Volodin version the triangular subgroups are indexed by orderings of a finite basis. The realization \(S(A)\) of the specified stable complex satisfies \(K_i(A)\cong\pi_{i-1}S(A)\) for \(i\ge1\), with \(\pi_0\) carrying its stable group structure.
reconstruction: The source's two-sided formulation and its marginal restrictions are recorded without claiming that each possible choice of conjugating matrices gives literally the same complex. The standard Volodin model is the precise comparator. The homotopy groups belong to a realization, not to an ordinary discrete general linear group.
fate: The construction had appeared in \citet{volodin1971extraordinary}, received on 27 July 1970 and published in 1971. Its relationship with Vaserstein's relative formulation is specified in \citet[\S15, Theorem 15.1 and Corollary 15.1]{vaserstein1976foundations}; the later comparison with Quillen is a separate theorem, indexed under record 257.
present_status: As of November 2026: the simplicial models are established. The unreadable adjective in the margin is not used to impose a new matrix restriction.

title: The algebraic cone and suspension rings
notes: The notation \(\ell A\) denotes infinite matrices with finite rows and columns; \(MA\) denotes the finite matrices, and \(\mu A=\ell A/MA\) is called the ring of Fredholm operators.
statement: Let \(C(A)\) be the ring of countably indexed matrices over \(A\) having finitely many nonzero entries in each row and each column, and let \(M_\infty(A)\) be its ideal of matrices with finite total support. Set \(\Sigma A=C(A)/M_\infty(A)\). Matrix multiplication is well-defined under these finiteness conditions. The invertible classes in the quotient are algebraic Fredholm classes; arbitrary elements of the quotient need not be invertible.
reconstruction: The symbols \(C\) and \(\Sigma\) replace the source's \(\ell\) and \(\mu\). This purely algebraic quotient is analogous to a Calkin algebra. Even over \(\mathbb C\), row and column finiteness alone does not ensure that the matrix defines a bounded operator on \(\ell^2\).
fate: The matrix cone is treated in \citet[\S\S3--4 and Chapter IV]{vaserstein1976foundations}. Its historical introduction credits earlier Fredholm-operator definitions of negative K-groups to Karoubi--Villamayor and Wagoner; the 1972 talk reuses that algebraic construction.
present_status: As of November 2026: standard algebraic suspension construction, with the ring and its group of invertible classes distinguished.

title: Suspension, vanishing of cone K-theory, and the index
notes: The framed theorem is \(K_iA=K_{i+1}\mu A\), in particular \(K_1\mu A=K_0A\), called the index. Its explanation is contractibility of \(GL(\ell A)\), or at least vanishing of \(K_i(\ell A)\). A separate sentence asks whether this holds for Quillen's functor.
statement: For a unital associative ring \(A\), the algebraic cone is flasque: the stable sum swindle gives \(K_n(C(A))=0\). The extension \(M_\infty(A)\to C(A)\to\Sigma A\), together with Morita invariance and its applicable localization sequence, gives \[K_{n+1}(\Sigma A)\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }K_n(A)\] as an isomorphism for \(n\ge0\), and for every integer \(n\) in nonconnective K-theory. For \(n=0\), \(\partial\) is the algebraic index.
reconstruction: Contractibility refers to the chosen K-theory or simplicial model; it is not a claim that the underlying discrete ring or group is contractible. The special matrix ideal supplies the exactness required here, without asserting excision for arbitrary ideals. The exercise about finding the arrows is interpreted as supplying these boundary and comparison maps, not as an additional specified problem.
fate: The degree shift and comparison are announced in \citet[the first theorem block, p.231]{vaserstein1973foundations}, received on 14 November 1972, and developed in \citet[Chapter IV, especially \S18; \S27]{vaserstein1976foundations}. The latter explicitly dates the comparison programme to Gelfand's seminar in spring 1972. The same degree shift holds in Quillen K-theory under the displayed hypotheses.
present_status: As of November 2026: resolved. The question about Quillen's theory is an instance of the model-comparison problem GP-1971-21.

title: The unspecified Banach-ring generalization
notes: One line says that the theorem generalizes to a Banach ring and gives the usual theorem. No topology, completed ideal, or K-theory convention is named.
statement: A Banach-ring analogue must specify the category of modules or operators, its completion, the ideal being divided out, and whether K-theory uses norm-continuous paths or algebraic plus constructions. The preceding row-and-column-finite ring is not, as defined, a Banach algebra. Thus this line does not determine a single comparison or periodicity theorem.
reconstruction: An analytic Fredholm-index theorem is a plausible context, but identifying it with a particular completed Calkin extension would supply data not present in the source. Algebraic and topological K-groups of a Banach algebra are not silently equated.
fate: The verified matrix construction in \citet[Chapter IV]{vaserstein1976foundations} and the searches for Karoubi--Villamayor Banach-ring versions provide context, but no exact Banach theorem with the notebook's omitted choices was identified.
present_status: As of November 2026: unidentified at the required level of hypotheses; the ambiguity does not establish an open analytic problem.

title: Free rings are K-acyclic only in the reduced convention
notes: A framed statement says \(K_i(\text{free ring})=0\), followed immediately by the warning that there is no contraction of the free ring.
statement: If \(F\) is a free associative nonunital ring on a set \(X\), its unitization is \(\mathbb Z\langle X\rangle\). The relevant assertion is \[\ker\!\left(K_n(\mathbb Z\langle X\rangle)\longrightarrow K_n(\mathbb Z)\right)=0.\] Equivalently the inclusion of constants induces \(K_n(\mathbb Z)\cong K_n(\mathbb Z\langle X\rangle)\). This holds for all integers in the nonconnective extension. It does not assert \(K_0(\mathbb Z\langle X\rangle)=0\), nor a contraction by ring homomorphisms.
reconstruction: The augmentation and reduced interpretation are supplied from the surrounding free nonunital resolution. No excision identification with an arbitrary ambient relative group is required. This is the same acyclicity used in occurrences 1971-253.3--1971-253.4.
fate: See \citet[the second theorem block, p.231]{vaserstein1973foundations}, followed by \citet[Theorem 28.1 and Corollary 28.1]{vaserstein1976foundations}. The detailed article explains that the higher-degree argument uses Gersten's results and does not reproduce that long proof. The 1972 announcement and the 1973/1976 publications are therefore distinguished.
present_status: As of November 2026: established in the stated reduced sense. The free-ring vanishing supports the normalized universal-relation question GP-1971-20, but is stronger than that degree-two instance.

title: Free resolutions and the required relative degree shift
notes: For \(0\to L'\to L\to A\to0\), with \(L\) free, the notes write \(K_iA=K_{i-1}L'\), refer to a long exact sequence, and say that induction gives the theories of Swan and Gersten.
statement: Let \(F(A)\twoheadrightarrow A\) be a functorial free nonunital presentation. The homotopy fibre of \(K(F(A))\to K(A)\) has homotopy groups \(K_{n+1}(A)\), since the reduced K-space of \(F(A)\) is contractible. It must be modeled as relative K-theory. In Vaserstein's explicit ring recursion, the doubled fibre product \(D(A)=F(A)\times_A F(A)\), together with the split projection to \(F(A)\), supplies the functor used to shift degrees. The assertion for the bare kernel \(L'\) does not follow from free acyclicity alone.
reconstruction: The relative fibre replaces the source's unrestricted use of \(K(L')\). This is the same excision issue as occurrence 1971-253.8. A long exact sequence is legitimate for the homotopy fibre by definition; identifying its terms with absolute K-groups of an ideal needs an additional theorem.
fate: \citet[\S29, definition preceding Theorem 29.1 and Theorem 29.1]{vaserstein1976foundations} gives the precise doubled-ring recursion and comparison with Gersten and Swan. The comparison was announced in \citet{vaserstein1973foundations}, following the spring 1972 seminar.
present_status: As of November 2026: the corrected relative construction is established. The bare-kernel shortcut remains an unjustified literal statement in the notes.

title: Agreement with Bass negative groups and regular vanishing
notes: The final lines say that the groups with negative index also coincide with Bass's, and that all of them vanish for regular rings.
statement: For a unital ring, the negative groups obtained from repeated algebraic suspension agree with Bass negative K-theory. If \(A\) is regular noetherian, then \(K_n(A)=0\) for all \(n<0\). Here regular means the homological regularity relevant to the fundamental theorem, not merely absence of zero divisors.
reconstruction: The regular noetherian hypothesis is made explicit to avoid extending the assertion to arbitrary singular domains. The equality concerns negative K-groups, separately from the positive polynomial-homotopy comparison on P000422.
fate: Bass's negative construction predates the lecture; its relationship with the Fredholm model is recalled in \citet[introduction, pp.95--96 and Chapter IV]{vaserstein1976foundations}. The modern nonconnective formulation is \citet[IV, \S10]{weibel2013kbook}; the regularity convention is already explicit in \citet{basshellerswan1964whitehead}.
present_status: As of November 2026: classical. Singular rings can have nonzero negative K-groups, so the regularity qualification carries mathematical content.

title: Karoubi–Villamayor comparison: a domain hypothesis is insufficient
notes: The first two lines say that Karoubi's positive-index theory differs from Bass's, but coincides when there are no zero divisors: \ru{Нет делит. нуля}.
statement: For a unital ring \(A\), polynomial-homotopy K-theory is \(KV_n(A)=\pi_{n-1}GL(A[\Delta^\bullet])\), \(n\ge1\). The natural comparison \(K_n(A)\to KV_n(A)\) is an isomorphism for regular noetherian rings. It is not an isomorphism for all integral domains. For example, the graded domain \(A=\mathbb F_p[t^2,t^3]\) has \(KV_2(A)=KV_2(\mathbb F_p)=0\), whereas \(K_2(A,(t^2,t^3))\ne0\) and hence \(K_2(A)\ne0\).
reconstruction: The intended correct hypothesis is reconstructed as regularity, not read into the words ``no zero divisors''. \ours\ The diagnostic deduction is as follows. Fix a prime \(p\) and the perfect field \(k=\mathbb F_p\). The ring \(A=k[t^2,t^3]\subset k[t]\) is a domain, and \(t^2\mapsto s^2t^2,\ t^3\mapsto s^3t^3\) defines a polynomial homotopy from the augmentation followed by constants to the identity. Hence \(KV_2(A)=KV_2(k)=K_2(k)=0\). In Hesselholt--Nikolaus's Theorem A, take \(a=2,b=3,r=1\). The truncation set contains 1, and the first Witt coordinate maps its quotient onto \(k\), since the images of both Verschiebung maps \(V_2,V_3\) have zero first coordinate. Thus \(K_2(A,(t^2,t^3))\ne0\). The augmentation is split, so this relative group is a direct summand of \(K_2(A)\); indeed it is the whole group because \(K_2(k)=0\).
fate: The distinction between polynomial paths and stable elementary equivalence predates the talk and is discussed in \citet[introduction, p.96]{vaserstein1976foundations}. The precise regular-ring comparison is \citet[IV, Theorem 11.8]{weibel2013kbook}. A direct modern counterexample to the literal domain claim follows from \citet[Theorem A]{hesselholtnikolaus2020cuspidal}: its Witt-vector quotient for \(a=2,b=3,r=1\) is nonzero. That paper first circulated on 20 March 2019 and was published in 2020; it is not attributed to the 1972 seminar.
present_status: As of November 2026: the regular-ring comparison is established, and the unrestricted domain claim is false. This is a correction of hypotheses, not a newly posed unresolved problem. The editorial counterexample deduction was independently checked against Theorem A, the split long exact sequence, and the polynomial contraction; it also applies in characteristics two and three.

title: The stable plus construction and its universal property
notes: With \(G=GL(A)\), the notes identify \(E(A)\) with the perfect commutator subgroup, give \(BG\to BG^+\) with fundamental group \(G/E\) and unchanged homology, and state universality for maps to H-spaces. Morava adds that an H-space hypothesis can be dropped when the other map induces a homology isomorphism.
statement: For a unital associative ring \(A\), \(E(A)=[GL(A),GL(A)]\) is perfect. The plus map \(BGL(A)\to BGL(A)^+\) kills \(E(A)\) and induces isomorphisms in homology with every local coefficient system pulled back from \(K_1(A)\). Its target is a homotopy-commutative H-space, and \(K_i(A)=\pi_iBGL(A)^+\), \(i\ge1\). The corresponding factorization property holds for connected H-space targets. A uniqueness comparison without an H-space assumption must retain the appropriate fundamental-group and acyclic-map hypotheses; an arbitrary integral homology equivalence alone is insufficient.
reconstruction: Local coefficients and the killed subgroup are supplied to make the plus characterization precise. Morava's abbreviated correction is interpreted only within that setting, not as a blanket homology-Whitehead theorem for all spaces. The crossed equality sign does not alter the verified stable perfectness statement.
fate: Quillen's construction was already reported in \citet[\S3, p.50]{quillen1971cohomology}, from the 1970 ICM lecture, printed in 1971. The precise characterization and universal properties are \citet[IV, Definition 1.1 and Theorems 1.5 and 1.8]{weibel2013kbook}. The explicit discussion continued in occurrence 1971-259.1.
present_status: As of November 2026: established. This exposition does not create a new comparison theorem merely because its catalogue attribution is uncertain.

title: Equality of the Quillen, Volodin, Swan, Gersten and Vaserstein groups
notes: The framed theorem states \(K_iA=K_i^QA\). Above the right-hand K-symbol the labels list Swan, Gersten, two Volodin constructions, and Vaserstein.
statement: For an associative ring \(A\) with identity and \(i\ge1\), the stable simplicial K-groups of the indicated Volodin and Vaserstein constructions, the free-resolution constructions of Swan and Gersten, and \(\pi_iBGL(A)^+\) are naturally isomorphic, when the nonunital intermediary rings and relative constructions use the respective published definitions. This does not identify Karoubi--Villamayor's polynomial-homotopy theory with Quillen's for arbitrary rings.
reconstruction: The unital hypothesis and the restriction to positive groups are stated explicitly. The list is treated as a comparison of constructions, not a claim that their underlying spaces are identical before completion or delooping. The preceding Karoubi warning is essential to the scope.
fate: The precise match is \citet[the first theorem block]{vaserstein1973foundations}; the detailed proof is \citet[\S15, \S27, Theorem 27.2, and \S29, Theorem 29.1]{vaserstein1976foundations}. The latter records first announcement in Gelfand's seminar in spring 1972 and in Tbilisi in autumn 1972; the short paper was received on 14 November 1972. Class B is relative to the conditional catalogue speaker Kazhdan; it does not imply an independent announcement distinct from Vaserstein's occurrences 1971-253.14 and 1971-256.3.
present_status: As of November 2026: resolved for the specified models and rings. GP-1971-21 links the earlier question and this report without duplicating its mathematical priority.

title: Acyclic coinvariants and the quotient comparison
notes: A diagram compares realization before and after quotienting the cone's simplicial matrix space by \(GL(MA)\). The final quotient is labeled \(BG^+\), with two exclamation marks. Bars and initial B-symbols are overwritten, so the individual nodes are not all diplomatically secure.
statement: The proof uses an equivariant simplicial model and its chain complex, not an unrestricted rule that taking a quotient commutes with geometric realization. In Vaserstein's formulation, if every finite subset of a ring \(R\) lies in a unital subring, the coinvariant chain complex \((C_*S(R))_{GL(R)}\), with his stable-matrix notation understood, has vanishing positive-degree homology. Applying this acyclicity to the cone comparison, together with the kernel on \(\pi_1\), identifies the resulting connected target as a plus construction.
reconstruction: The explicitly published acyclicity theorem is supplied as the rigorous content behind the sketch. The point-set quotient, simplicial quotient, and their realizations remain distinct until the hypotheses and comparison maps are verified. No overwritten B-symbol is silently resolved into a different proof.

title: The first three K-groups of a finite field
notes: For a finite field \(F_q\), the notes give \(K_0(F_q)=\mathbb Z\), \(K_1(F_q)=F_q^*\), and say that \(K_2(F_q)=0\) is easy to show.
statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power. Dimension induces \(K_0(\mathbb F_q)\cong\mathbb Z\), determinant induces \(K_1(\mathbb F_q)\cong\mathbb F_q^\times\cong\mathbb Z/(q-1)\), and \(K_2(\mathbb F_q)=0\). The dimension and determinant identifications are canonical; an isomorphism of the multiplicative group with a chosen cyclic group requires choosing a generator.

fate: The low-degree groups were already part of the theory of Bass, Steinberg and Milnor; Quillen's announcement explicitly says that his definition agrees with Bass and Milnor \citep[\S3, p.50]{quillen1971cohomology}. title: Quillen’s complete finite-field calculation

title: K-theory of the algebraic closure and its apparent periodicity
notes: The displayed formula over \(\overline F_q\) gives vanishing positive even groups and identifies odd groups with \(\overline F_q^*\), followed by ``like the periodicity theorem''. The first odd index is overwritten and provisionally \(2i+1\).
statement: For \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p\), \(K_0(k)=\mathbb Z\), and for every \(i\ge1\), \[K_{2i}(k)=0,\qquad K_{2i-1}(k)\cong\bigoplus_{\ell\ne p}\mathbb Q_\ell/\mathbb Z_\ell.\] Each odd group is abstractly isomorphic to \(k^\times\). title: Frobenius invariants recover the finite-field orders
notes: The continuation says only that the Frobenius automorphism is used.
statement: For \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p\), arithmetic Frobenius \(x\mapsto x^p\) acts on \(K_{2i-1}(k)\) as multiplication by \(p^i\). Thus \(x\mapsto x^q\), with \(q=p^a\), acts as multiplication by \(q^i\). Extension of scalars identifies \(K_{2i-1}(\mathbb F_q)\) with the subgroup of Galois invariants in \(K_{2i-1}(k)\); this is the kernel of multiplication by \(q^i-1\), cyclic of that order. For finite intermediate extensions the restriction-of-scalars map corresponds to the norm on these invariant groups.

fate: All the functorial assertions appear in \citet[\S3, Theorem 2, p.51]{quillen1971cohomology}. They sharpen the group-only formulas in the preceding two items and were already available before the lecture.
